title: CB-Dock3: an enhanced web server for protein-ligand blind docking.
journal: Nucleic Acids Research (2026), PMCID PMC13355045, PMID 42087554

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Ran paper_context.py: no GEO/SRA/BioProject accessions, no Zenodo/Dryad deposit, and the only text-mined accession is PDB 5WZU (an example structure). The Europe PMC supplementaryFiles endpoint timed out (75 s, then a HEAD at 120 s), so the supplement could not be retrieved. A HEAD on the server URL returned HTTP 200 (49-byte HTML stub). There is no downloadable dataset to open.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The data availability statement lists only the web server. The benchmark is CASF-2016 (a public 285-complex docking test set built from PDBbind 2016), with 192/285 complexes docked within 2.0 Å RMSD (root-mean-square deviation of atom positions), i.e. a 67.4% success rate. Supplementary Table S1 reportedly holds per-complex results. The metal-aware scoring terms were fitted on PDBbind 2020 metal complexes.

a1_downloadable.note: No dataset is deposited. The paper offers a web server, not data. The supplement could not be retrieved (Europe PMC endpoint timed out), and it is described as per-complex benchmark results only. Checked by repository search and a server HEAD.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: No new label exists. The only table (Table S1, per the paper) holds CB-Dock3's own pose RMSD on CASF-2016, which is a tool output, not a biological measurement. Any binding label would have to come from PDBbind, not from this paper.

a3_inputs_present.note: Not checked. CASF-2016 structures are public elsewhere, but they are not part of this paper's data.

a4_units_stated.note: Not checked. RMSD in Å per the paper text.

a5_enough_rows.note: The paper says the benchmark has 285 complexes, far below the ~400-row floor even for classification. Rows were not counted because the supplement could not be retrieved.

a8_label_provenance.note: Per-complex success or RMSD values come from the docking program's own predictions. Modelling them would mean predicting another tool's error, not biology.

c2_audit.note: Not searched: evaluation stopped at Part A. The paper itself cites DiffDock and AlphaFold 3 as ML docking methods; the empty list does not mean the field is empty (it is in fact crowded).

backbone.name: none applicable (no dataset)
backbone.licence: web server free to use; no data licence stated

integration.partner_dataset: PDBbind / CASF-2016 (where the benchmark complexes actually come from)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Not assessed: stopped at Part A.

honest_claim_h3: Not assessed: stopped at Part A. The best possible claim would be 'predicts when CB-Dock3 fails on 285 CASF-2016 complexes', which is too small and tool-specific to be worth making.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use protein-ligand complex structures to predict whether a docking program will place the drug-like molecule in the right pose.
plain_idea.train_on: Per-complex docking results on the CASF-2016 benchmark, about 285 complexes per the paper (not verified; supplement not retrievable).
plain_idea.predict: Whether CB-Dock3's predicted pose lands within 2 Å of the crystal structure. The true answer is the program's own RMSD against the experimental structure.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Little: it would only tell CB-Dock3 users when to trust a pose, and 285 examples cannot support a reliable model.

ml_idea: None viable. This is a web-server paper with no new dataset; the only table is about 285 per-complex benchmark outcomes of the tool itself.

effort.compute_note: Not estimated; rejected at Part A.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Already failed: the data availability statement lists only the web server, and the paper's benchmark has 285 complexes.

verdict_reason: Tool paper with no deposited dataset (A1). Its only table, about 285 CASF-2016 docking outcomes, is the tool's own output (A8) and too small (A5). Protein-ligand pose prediction is also crowded with open ML models such as DiffDock.
